item.title: Hachinohe Emburi: Aomori's Ancient Winter Rite — Guide
item.description: The Hachinohe Emburi is one of Japan’s most unusual major festivals — an ancient rice-planting ceremony held February 17–20, where farmers wearing magnificent horse-head headdresses (eboshi) dance to pray for a bountiful harvest. Over 800 years old, it feels genuinely archaic and remains almost unknown to foreign visitors. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Hachinohe, Aomori Hours Feb 17–20 (daytime performances) Admission Mostly free; some paid indoor shows Time needed 1–2 hours Best time February 17–20 (fixed) Highlights Dancers in dramatic horse-head headdresses (eboshi).

item.title: Towada Snow Lantern Festival: Aomori's Winter Glow — Guide
item.description: Each February, the zelkova-lined Kancho Street in Towada City fills with hundreds of hand-crafted snow lanterns and kamakura (snow-igloo) shrines, lit by candlelight at dusk. Snow sculptures, warm amazake and craft stalls complete one of Tohoku’s most intimate and atmospheric winter events. 🗓️ At a Glance Location Towada City, Aomori Hours February, evenings Admission Free Time needed 1–1.

item.title: Asahikawa Winter Festival Guide: Snow Sculptures & Zoo
item.description: Hokkaido’s second city, Asahikawa, is one of Japan’s coldest places — and it embraces winter wholeheartedly. Each February, the Asahikawa Winter Festival raises some of the largest snow sculptures in Japan (it has held world records), with huge snow stages, slides and illuminations along the Ishikari River and downtown. The city is also home to the wildly popular Asahiyama Zoo, famous for its winter penguin walk, and is a hub for Asahikawa-style soy ramen and a gateway to the Daisetsuzan mountains.
